context:
Multiprogramming in Operating Systems

Multiprogramming allows multiple programs to run simultaneously by switching between them to maximize CPU utilization. While one program is waiting (e.g., for I/O operations), the CPU can execute another program. This ensures the system is efficient and avoids CPU idle time. Examples of multiprogramming in real-world applications include web servers handling multiple user requests at once, banking systems enabling ATMs and online banking to function together, and healthcare systems managing patient data, billing, and inventory simultaneously.
Disadvantages of Batch Systems

Batch systems process jobs in groups without user interaction. A major disadvantage is that users cannot interact with the job once it’s submitted, which delays changes or corrections. For instance, in payroll systems, urgent updates to employee data cannot be applied immediately. Debugging is another challenge, as errors are only identified after the batch is processed, potentially delaying all tasks. Additionally, these systems may leave resources underutilized when jobs involve slow I/O operations, resulting in idle CPU time.
Parallel vs. Distributed Systems

Parallel systems involve multiple processors working on a single task simultaneously, often sharing memory and resources within a single system. An example is a supercomputer used for weather forecasting. Distributed systems, on the other hand, consist of independent systems working together over a network to solve problems, such as cloud platforms like AWS or Google Cloud. While parallel systems focus on speed and performance for a single task, distributed systems prioritize resource sharing and handling separate tasks.
Hard vs. Soft Real-Time Systems

In hard real-time systems, tasks must meet strict deadlines, and missing them can cause catastrophic failures. For example, aircraft control systems must respond instantly to ensure safety. In contrast, soft real-time systems aim to meet deadlines but are more flexible if some delays occur. An example is video streaming, where slight delays may lower quality but do not stop the service altogether.
